places.name: San Ysidro Port of Entry
places.text: Interstate 5 begins at the Mexican border, at the San Ysidro Port of Entry, which federal officials call the busiest land port in the Western Hemisphere. On a typical day about 70,000 vehicles and 20,000 people on foot enter the United States here from Tijuana, with cars lining up across 34 lanes.
places.more: There has been a border inspection station in San Ysidro since the early 1900s, and a Mission Revival customs house from the early 1930s still stands and holds offices. The main port was built in 1973, and a $741 million rebuild that took nearly ten years was finished in 2019. Trucks have crossed at the Otay Mesa port since 1983. The lanes into Mexico now pass through a Mexican gateway called El Chaparral, which roughly tripled them to 22. Waits to enter the United States can still stretch to several hours.

places.name: Kumeyaay homeland
places.text: This is the homeland of the Kumeyaay Nation. Kumeyaay country runs from the Pacific to the Colorado River, and along the coast from about Oceanside to south of Ensenada, so since 1848 the international border has run right through it. Kumeyaay people live on both sides today, with 13 bands in San Diego County and more communities in Baja California.
places.more: Kumeyaay tradition holds that the people have lived around San Diego since 10,000 BC. The Spanish called them Diegueños, after Mission San Diego, and in Mexico they are known as Kumiai. Before Cabrillo landed in 1542, trail runners carrying messages between bands had already spread word of the strangers. Families and ceremonies still cross the line, and about 1,900 Kumiai came to hold special visas to attend events on the US side. Bird songs, which recount migrations and ancestral history, are still sung at gatherings. In 2020, as border wall construction sped up, Kumeyaay women led protests, and the La Posta Band sued to stop building through a sacred burial ground.

places.name: Tijuana River
places.text: The Tijuana River rises in the mountains of Baja California, runs through Tijuana in a concrete channel, and crosses into the United States near here for its last few miles to the sea. Its mouth, the Tijuana River Estuary, is Southern California's largest coastal wetland, where more than 370 kinds of birds have been seen. The river also carries Tijuana's sewage overflows, and in 2013 beaches near its mouth were closed for 204 days.
places.more: The river runs only after rains, and it floods. Floods in 1891 and 1895 washed out Tia Juana City, an 1887 settlement where the outlet mall by the border stands now. In 1908, William Smythe started the Little Landers colony nearby, where each member farmed about 2 acres and all the buying and selling was shared. The colony took the name San Ysidro, an old spelling of Saint Isidore the Laborer, and lasted until a great flood wiped out its farms in 1916. Today a regional park of more than 1,800 acres fills much of the valley, with trails for walking and horseback riding, and big winter waves off the river mouth have drawn surfers since at least 1937. In 2020, a trade agreement set aside $300 million to fight the river's pollution.

places.name: Montgomery's Silver Wing
places.text: East of the freeway, a 93-foot stainless steel test wing for a World War II bomber stands on end. Locals sometimes call it the Silver Wing. It honors John J. Montgomery, who in the spring of 1884 made glider flights of up to 600 feet from the rim of Otay Mesa. He never claimed to be first, but some historians count these as the first controlled flights of a heavier-than-air craft in America.
places.more: Montgomery shaped his first glider's wing on the curve of a seagull's. He steered it up and down with a movable elevator and tipped it side to side by shifting his weight. The glider handled side gusts poorly, so he studied turkey vultures and gave his next glider hinged wing flaps, an early form of the ailerons on airplanes today. The Montgomerys' 1880s Fruitland Ranch stood where this freeway now runs, and in 1949 the road from the border to downtown San Diego was named the John J. Montgomery Freeway. He later taught at Santa Clara College and died in a glider crash in San Jose in 1911. The memorial was dedicated in 1950.
places.spot: Look for a giant silver airplane wing standing straight up like a tower.

places.name: The rainmaker's flood
places.text: In 1915, San Diego's city council voted to pay Charles Hatfield, a self-styled rainmaker, $10,000 to fill a reservoir. In January 1916 the rain came and kept coming. On January 27 the Lower Otay Dam burst and sent a wall of water 40 feet high down the Otay River valley, which meets San Diego Bay near here. The flood reportedly killed about 20 people, though accounts vary, among them 11 Japanese American farmers.
places.more: Hatfield called himself a moisture accelerator. He brewed a secret mix of 23 chemicals in evaporating tanks, and for San Diego he built a tower beside Lake Morena. The storms overflowed the Sweetwater Dam too, washed away bridges, stranded trains and cut phone lines. Afterward the council refused to pay unless Hatfield accepted the blame for damages, with claims already at $3.5 million. He sued, and in 1938 the courts ruled the rain an act of God, so he was cleared but never paid. A San Diego mayor who studied his record called him nothing more than a darned good weather prophet.

places.name: South Bay Salt Works
places.text: On the bay side of the freeway, ocean water sits in ponds until the sun dries it into salt. People have harvested salt here since at least 1871, which makes the South Bay Salt Works the second-longest-running business in San Diego, after the San Diego Union-Tribune newspaper. Its ponds cover more than a thousand acres and yield about 75,000 tons of salt a year.
places.more: On the West Coast, only San Francisco Bay and San Diego Bay have the natural conditions for making sea salt. The very salty ponds breed brine shrimp and brine flies, a feast for birds, and they sit inside the San Diego Bay National Wildlife Refuge. Ninety-four kinds of birds use the area, and a 2010 count found more than 20,000 birds, including endangered California least terns. The 1916 flood wiped out the ponds, and rebuilding took until the 1950s. As late as 1978 the works supplied the salt for San Diego's tuna fleet. When its little narrow-gauge salt railway was torn out in the 1970s, the spot where it crossed over a full-size railroad was kept, the only such crossing in the United States.

places.name: Chula Vista, the old Lemon Capital
places.text: Chula Vista is Spanish for beautiful view, a name suggested by the designer of the Sweetwater Dam. Water from that dam, finished in 1888, irrigated the farmland here, and for a time Chula Vista was the largest lemon-growing center in the world. By 1911 about 4,000 acres were lemon groves, and the town was once known as the Lemon Capital of the World.
places.more: Lemons were introduced by a retired professor from the University of Wisconsin. By 1911 growers earned about $2,000 an acre, and lemon sales topped $400,000 a year. Japanese American farmers made celery a big crop too, and in 1931 lemons brought in $1 million and celery $600,000. Then, in 1941, Rohr Aircraft moved to town, and its 11,000 workers built power units for B-24 Liberator bombers. With workers off at war or at the factory, the farmland was sold, and the groves never came back. The city's Lemon Festival still pays tribute to them.

places.name: Sweetwater Marsh
places.text: West of the freeway, where the Sweetwater River meets San Diego Bay, 316 acres of salt marsh and coastal upland form part of a national wildlife refuge. More than 90 percent of the bay's old wetlands have been filled, drained or diked, which is why this piece matters. The refuge breeds endangered light-footed Ridgway's rails, and it is the only place in the United States where a plant called yerba reuma grows wild.
places.more: The Kumeyaay fished, hunted and gathered here. From 1916 to 1920, the Hercules Powder Company ran a 30-acre plant on this shore, turning kelp into acetone and potash, a key ingredient in smokeless gunpowder during World War I. The site is now known as Gunpowder Point. The refuge also holds the Living Coast Discovery Center, a zoo and aquarium that opened in 1987 as the Chula Vista Nature Interpretive Center, with green sea turtles, sharks, rays and bald and golden eagles. Trails lead 1.5 miles out to the bay, and more than 200 kinds of birds have been recorded on the refuge.
places.wiki: San Diego Bay National Wildlife Refuge

places.name: National City's royal ranch
places.text: National City takes its name from a ranch. Spanish soldiers grazed their horses on 26,000 acres here called El Rancho del Rey, the Ranch of the King. After Mexico won independence it became Rancho de la Nación, the Ranch of the Nation. In 1868 three Kimball brothers from San Francisco bought the whole rancho and kept the name National for the town they founded.
places.more: Frank Kimball's house had a bathtub and hot running water, and it was called the first modern house in the county. The brothers built the area's first roads and railroad, a post office and a wharf. In 1882 the California Southern Railroad built a depot here, the first Pacific Coast terminal of the Santa Fe Railway. When transcontinental trains arrived in November 1885, one of the biggest land booms in California history began. The Italianate depot is the only survivor of the five original transcontinental terminal stations. Later, sailors' bars earned National Avenue the nickname Mile of Bars, and the city remade it as the Mile of Cars, one of the first auto malls in the world.

places.name: Naval Base San Diego
places.text: The Navy ships along the bay belong to Naval Base San Diego, the main home port of the US Pacific Fleet. More than 50 ships tie up at its 13 piers, and over 24,000 military personnel and 10,000 civilians work on the base. It is the second-largest surface ship base in the world, after Naval Station Norfolk.
places.more: In 1918, a company building concrete ships for World War I used this shore. When that business faded, the Navy took over, and in February 1922 the site opened as the Destroyer Base, San Diego. In 1924 alone, it took 77 destroyers out of service. During World War II it was renamed the Repair Base, and from 1943 to 1945 its crews repaired, overhauled or converted more than 5,000 ships. It became the Pacific Fleet's main home port after the Long Beach Naval Shipyard closed in 1994. National City's three-mile bayfront is part of the base.
places.spot: Look for big Navy ships tied up at the piers along the bay.

places.name: Coronado Bridge and Chicano Park
places.text: The long, curving bridge over the bay is the San Diego-Coronado Bridge, opened in 1969. The Navy wanted 200 feet of clearance for its ships, so the bridge curves 80 degrees to gain enough length to climb that high at a reasonable grade. Under its ramps, beside this freeway, lies Chicano Park, home to the largest collection of outdoor murals in the United States.
places.more: Barrio Logan, a mostly Mexican American neighborhood, was split in two when this freeway came through in 1963, and the bridge ramps divided it again in 1969. More than 5,000 homes and businesses were removed. The city promised a park, but on April 22, 1970, a student named Mario Solis found bulldozers preparing a Highway Patrol parking lot instead. Neighbors and students occupied the land for twelve days, planting trees, flowers and cactus, until the city agreed to build the park. Artist Salvador Torres proposed turning the gray concrete pillars into a giant canvas, and painting began in 1973. The park became a National Historic Landmark in 2016, and every April the neighborhood celebrates Chicano Park Day.
places.spot: Look for a long bridge curving high over the bay toward Coronado.

places.name: Lindbergh Field
places.text: Jets landing at San Diego International Airport make a steep descent over the crest of Bankers Hill, close to the downtown towers, to reach a single runway. It is the busiest single-runway airport in the United States. Because the airport is so close, federal rules since the 1970s have kept downtown buildings to 500 feet or less, which is why the skyline looks so even.
places.more: In 1927 the Ryan company built the Spirit of St. Louis near here for Charles Lindbergh's flight across the Atlantic. Proud of that, San Diego voted bonds in 1928 for an airport, and Lindbergh lent it his name. It was dedicated that August as Lindbergh Field, while 140 Navy and 82 Army planes flew over. During World War II, Consolidated Aircraft built warplanes next door, and a street here is still named Liberator Way, after its B-24 Liberator. The name changed to San Diego International Airport in 2003. Most landings come in from the east, over downtown, because the usual winds blow from the west, and a curfew fines takeoffs between 11:30 at night and 6:30 in the morning.
places.spot: Look for a jet sliding down low over the rooftops toward the runway.

places.name: El Indio
places.text: El Indio began in 1940 as a family tortilla shop, and since 1947 it has served food from a spot on India Street that now sits beside the freeway. During World War II, workers from the aircraft factory across the street asked founder Ralph Pesqueira Sr. for a portable lunch. He adapted his Sonoran grandmother's recipe for flautas, and he claimed credit for naming the little rolled tacos taquitos.
places.more: The first shop, at India and Grape streets, made tortillas by hand. In 1947 the family moved to 3695 India Street and began selling taquitos and other Sonoran-style dishes. Los Angeles has a rival claim to the taquito's early days: Cielito Lindo, opened on Olvera Street in 1934. The Pesqueira family still runs El Indio.

places.name: Old Town and Presidio Hill
places.text: The hill east of the freeway is Presidio Hill, where Spain founded its first fort and mission in California in 1769, above Kosa'aay, a Kumeyaay village of 30 to 40 families. In the 1820s, settlers moved down to the foot of the hill and started a town. That town is preserved as Old Town San Diego State Historic Park, with five original adobes, and the park and its museums are free to enter.
places.more: When the Portolá expedition arrived in 1769, the crews of its supply ships were dying of scurvy and thirst, and the people of Kosa'aay, whose name means drying out place, gave them food and water. The Spanish then set up a hospital camp on the hill and took over the village's water source, and less than a month after the mission was founded, the Kumeyaay fought back. In 1774 the mission moved a few miles up the valley, where Mission San Diego de Alcalá still stands. Old Town was the heart of San Diego until the 1860s, when Alonzo Horton's New Town by the harbor, today's downtown, drew people away. The Spanish Revival Serra Museum on the hilltop was given to the city by George Marston in 1929, and nothing of the old fort survives above ground.

places.name: Mission Bay and San Diego River
places.text: The San Diego River, crossed by the freeway near here, ends at the sea beside Mission Bay. The explorer Cabrillo named this water False Bay in 1542, when it was a shifting maze of lagoons and tidal marsh. Starting in the late 1940s, dredges moved 25 million cubic yards of sand and silt to build the islands and coves of Mission Bay Park, the largest man-made aquatic park in the country.
places.more: The river has wandered. Before 1821 it usually emptied into San Diego Bay, until a flood that fall swung it into False Bay in a single night, though no rain fell on the coast. Because its mud threatened to fill the harbor, Army engineers built an earth dike from near Old Town toward Point Loma in the 1850s. Storms washed part of it out, and only a rebuilt levee in the 1870s kept the river out of the harbor for good. The name Mission Bay comes from an 1888 poem by Rose Hartwick Thorpe. Dredging left only about 5 percent of the old wetlands. On September 25, 1974, Mission Bay hosted the first modern race to be called a triathlon, with 46 athletes.
places.spot: Look for boats on the calm water of Mission Bay.

places.name: Mount Soledad and Rose Canyon
places.text: The big hill west of the freeway is Mount Soledad, 823 feet high, with a 29-foot cross and TV towers on top. Its steep north and east slopes rise along the Rose Canyon Fault, which runs north from downtown San Diego beneath this freeway. The fault's last big quake probably struck in the 1700s, before the missions were built, and scientists estimate it produces a magnitude 6.9 quake about every 700 years on average.
places.more: Rose Canyon, which gave the fault its name, honors Louis Rose, a German Jewish immigrant who arrived in 1850 and was San Diego's first known Jewish resident. In 1853 he bought 650 acres in the canyon for a ranch and a tannery, and when people doubted San Diego's future, he would say, just wait a while and you will see. Before the Spanish came, the Kumeyaay village of Jamo stood on Rose Creek at the mouth of the canyon. The cross on the summit, dedicated in 1954, was fought over in court for about 25 years as a religious symbol on public land, until a private memorial association bought the ground beneath it in 2015. Dr. Seuss spent his last years in a house on the mountain.
places.spot: Look for a big cross and tall TV towers on top of the hill.

places.name: San Diego California Temple
places.text: The white building with two tall spires beside the freeway is the San Diego California Temple of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Dedicated in 1993, it was the church's third temple in California. Its spires rise about 200 feet, and a gold-leaf statue of the angel Moroni stands on top of the eastern one.
places.more: About 720,000 people toured it during its open house in 1993, well over the 600,000 expected. Architect William S. Lewis designed it with Dennis and Shelly Hyndman, a Roman Catholic couple who had never been inside a Latter-day Saint temple, and they avoided Southern California staples like stucco, tile and arches. Counting four small spires at the base of each tower, there are ten spires in all. The white exterior is plaster mixed with marble chips. A renovation that began in 2023 cleaned off stains from freeway traffic and sea air and restored all 144 original art-glass windows, and the public toured the temple again in the summer of 2026.
places.spot: Look for a white building with two tall pointed spires and a gold statue.

places.name: Torrey Pines and Peñasquitos Lagoon
places.text: West of the freeway, Los Peñasquitos Lagoon, Spanish for the little cliffs, spreads about 500 acres of marsh beside bluffs where Torrey pines grow, the rarest pine in North America. This kind grows wild only here and on a small strip just north in Del Mar. Sea winds twist the exposed trees into shapes like giant bonsai.
places.more: The only other wild Torrey pines, a related kind, grow on Santa Rosa Island off Santa Barbara. In May 2026 a wildfire burned a third of that island, and park officials said 60 to 80 percent of its Torrey pines may die. The trees here are protected in Torrey Pines State Natural Reserve, 2,000 acres of cliffs and trails. It began in 1899, when George Marston persuaded the city to set aside 364 acres, and newspaperwoman Ellen Browning Scripps later bought more land and gave it to the city. A mature tree's roots can spread 246 feet. From the cliffs, gray and humpback whales can be seen during their migrations.

places.name: Del Mar racetrack
places.text: The racetrack and fairgrounds beside the San Dieguito River are where the turf meets the surf. Singer Bing Crosby and businessman William Quigley founded the track, and on opening day, July 3, 1937, Crosby himself stood at the main gate welcoming 15,000 fans. The 370-acre grounds are also home to the San Diego County Fair.
places.more: On August 12, 1938, the track held a $25,000 winner-take-all match race between Seabiscuit and Ligaroti, the first thoroughbred race NBC radio broadcast nationwide, and Seabiscuit won by a nose. Crosby helped write the song Where the Turf Meets the Surf that year to promote the track. In the 1920s the Navy built an airfield on the wetlands between the river, the track and this freeway's route, and during World War II Navy blimps flew from it on patrols to watch for enemy submarines. The state closed the airport in 1959, and its land went into building Interstate 5. Live racing runs from July into early September, with a second meet in November.
places.spot: Look for the long tan grandstand of the racetrack near the ocean.

places.name: San Elijo Lagoon
places.text: The freeway crosses San Elijo Lagoon, a 915-acre reserve where Escondido Creek meets the sea. The Portolá expedition named it San Alejo, for Saint Alexius, in 1769. When this freeway was built in 1965, its earth berm squeezed the tides. The freeway and rail bridges have since been rebuilt with wider spans, and restored channels now let up to three times more water flow in and out with each tide.
places.more: People gathered food along this shore for at least 8,500 years, and their shell heaps hold scallops, clams, shark and abalone. It is Kumeyaay land, and Kumeyaay families once moved between the coast and inland with the seasons. A railroad berm came in 1887 and a coast highway in 1891, and from 1880 to 1940 dikes made room for duck hunting, salt making and sewage ponds. The $120 million restoration was paid for by TransNet, a half-cent local tax. Today the reserve counts about 300 kinds of birds and more than 300 kinds of plants. Its solar-powered nature center, built of recycled materials, opened in 2009, and parking is free.
places.spot: Look for the wide marsh and winding water channels beside the freeway.

places.name: Encinitas, the little oaks
places.text: Encinitas is Spanish for little oaks. In 1769 the Portolá expedition met people from the Kumeyaay village of Jeyal near San Elijo Lagoon and named this valley Los Encinos, for its oak forest. A Mexican land grant called Rancho Las Encinitas followed in 1842, and today's city formed in 1986 from five communities, including Cardiff-by-the-Sea, Leucadia and Olivenhain.
places.more: Its famous surf break, Swami's, is named for Paramahansa Yogananda, whose Self-Realization Fellowship temple has been a local landmark since the 1930s, and the break gets a mention in the Beach Boys song Surfin' U.S.A. In Cardiff, local surfers decided that a 16-foot bronze surfer statue called Magic Carpet Ride had terrible form, so they named it the Cardiff Kook, surfer slang for a wannabe. Pranksters keep dressing it up, in a lucha libre mask, an Uncle Sam suit, or the jaws of a papier-mâché shark. Cardiff's streets are named for British cities and classical composers, while Leucadia, named for the Greek island of Lefkada, has streets like Neptune, Phoebe and Daphne.

places.name: Ecke poinsettia ranch
places.text: The Ecke family moved their poinsettia business from Los Angeles to Encinitas in 1923, buying 40 acres at $150 an acre. By grafting two varieties together they grew fuller, bushier plants, and until the 1990s they had a virtual monopoly on the Christmas flower. As late as 2008, the family business still served about half the world market and 70 percent of the American one.
places.more: Albert Ecke, a German immigrant, began growing poinsettias in Los Angeles in 1909 and sold them from street stands. His son Paul worked out the grafting technique, and his grandson Paul Jr. tied the plant to Christmas by sending free poinsettias to TV stations to display from Thanksgiving to Christmas and by promoting them on The Tonight Show and Bob Hope's Christmas specials. Wild poinsettias grow from Mexico to Guatemala, and the Aztecs called the plant cuetlaxochitl. Despite its reputation it is not deadly: a survey of more than 20,000 poison center calls about poinsettias found no deaths. The family sold the business in 2012, and its Encinitas land went to the Leichtag Foundation.

places.name: Batiquitos Lagoon
places.text: The freeway crosses Batiquitos Lagoon, 610 acres of tidal wetland where San Marcos Creek meets the sea. Its name comes from batequi, a northwestern Mexican word for a watering hole dug in a streambed, borrowed from the Yaqui language. People have lived around this lagoon for more than 9,000 years.
places.more: After homesteaders arrived in the 1870s, a century of roads and building projects blocked the tides. The lagoon silted up and turned mostly fresh, and only five kinds of fish were left. A restoration that began in 1997 reopened it to the sea, and the lagoon has filled back up with life: more than 65 kinds of fish have since been found. Lagoons like this are nurseries for many ocean fish. A 1.75-mile nature trail follows the north shore, and it is friendly to strollers and wheelchairs.
places.spot: Look for the long lagoon stretching from the freeway toward the ocean.

places.name: The Flower Fields
places.text: In spring, the hillside east of the freeway turns bright with flowers. These are The Flower Fields, 55 acres of Giant Tecolote ranunculus, which bloom for six to eight weeks from early March into early May. The farm sits on a slope overlooking the Pacific and is open to visitors from March 1 until about Mother's Day.
places.more: Horticulturist Luther Gage brought ranunculus to the area in the 1920s, and decades later grower Edwin Frazee moved his ranunculus business to these coastal hillsides. Today the Ecke family of poinsettia fame owns the land, Mellano and Company grows the flowers, and the main crop is ranunculus bulbs. In 2012 the color mix of the flowers changed for the first time since 1997, and in 2015 the fields gained official protection from development. Nearby, Legoland California opened on March 20, 1999, the first Legoland park outside Europe.
places.spot: Look for a hillside covered in bright flowers in spring.

places.name: Carlsbad Strawberry Company
places.text: The strawberry fields beside the freeway at Cannon Road belong to the Carlsbad Strawberry Company, a pick-your-own farm run by third-generation farmer Jimmy Ukegawa. Seedlings go in each October, the first berries come around the start of the year, and picking season usually runs from March through July.
places.more: In the late 1990s the Ukegawa family's farm was struggling with rising costs, and in the early 2000s Jimmy began opening the fields for pick-your-own days. Today the Carlsbad Strawberry Company is one of San Diego's most popular pick-your-own farms. It grows a single variety, the Albion strawberry, and in fall its pumpkin patch can draw up to 1,500 people a night. In November 2006, Carlsbad voters approved Proposition D, Preserve the Flower and Strawberry Fields, which put a permanent open space designation on about 300 acres along both sides of Cannon Road, east of the freeway.
places.spot: Look for rows of strawberry plants in the fields beside the freeway.

places.name: Agua Hedionda and the desal plant
places.text: The freeway crosses Agua Hedionda Lagoon, Spanish for fetid water. Beside it, near the beach, the Claude Bud Lewis Carlsbad Desalination Plant opened in 2015 as the largest in the Western Hemisphere. It draws in about 100 million gallons of seawater a day and pushes it through reverse osmosis filters, turning half into drinking water, about 7 percent of what the San Diego region uses.
places.more: Before 1954 the lagoon was cut off from the ocean, a stinking pool at low tide. That year the new Encina Power Station opened it to the tides to cool its machinery, and dredging has kept it open since. The power plant, with its 400-foot smokestack, shut down in 2018 and was torn down between 2020 and 2022. The desalination plant took nearly 14 years to permit, design and build, cost about $1 billion with its pipelines, and survived five lawsuits from groups worried about energy use, brine and fish. It is named for Bud Lewis, Carlsbad's mayor for almost 25 years. Its extra-salty leftover water is diluted before it returns to the sea. The lagoon is critical habitat for the tidewater goby.
places.spot: Look for boats and paddleboards on the lagoon.

places.name: Carlsbad's mineral water
places.text: Carlsbad is named for a spa town in Bohemia. In the 1880s a former sailor, John Frazier, dug a well here and offered its water at the train stop, which became known as Frazier's Station. Tests on a second well found the water chemically similar to that of some of the world's most famous spas, so the town was named for the Bohemian spa of Karlsbad, now Karlovy Vary in the Czech Republic.
places.more: A land and mineral water company was formed to sell the water and the town, with a big campaign to bring visitors, and homes and shops went up through the 1880s. When land prices fell across the county in 1887, farms of citrus, avocados and olives kept the town going. The site of Frazier's first well can still be seen at Alt Karlsbad, a copy of a German Hanseatic house on Carlsbad Boulevard. Carlsbad became a city in 1952, to avoid being annexed by Oceanside. Inland, a 513-foot extinct volcano called Mount Calavera stands in a nature preserve.

places.name: Buena Vista Lagoon
places.text: The freeway crosses Buena Vista Lagoon, the 223-acre border between Carlsbad and Oceanside and California's first ecological reserve. A weir about 100 yards from the beach holds it back from the sea, so unlike its neighbors it is a freshwater lagoon. At least 103 kinds of birds have been seen here, and fall brings migrating flocks.
places.more: In the 1970s a flock of pink flamingos turned up on the lagoon. Locals were sure they had escaped from the San Diego Zoo, but the zoo always insisted it was missing none. For years people have debated whether to keep the lagoon fresh or open it to the ocean, as at nearby Agua Hedionda. The Buena Vista Audubon Society runs a nature center on its shore. Besides birds, the lagoon is home to 18 kinds of mammals and 14 kinds of reptiles and amphibians.
places.spot: Look for birds on the lagoon's open water.

places.name: Mission San Luis Rey
places.text: About four miles inland, on the banks of the San Luis Rey River, stands Mission San Luis Rey, founded in 1798 and nicknamed the King of the Missions. At its height its lands covered almost 950,400 acres, the largest of California's 21 missions. It lies in the homeland of the Payómkawichum, the People of the West, whom the Spanish named Luiseños after this mission.
places.more: Padre Fermín Lasuén founded it in June 1798 near the Luiseño village of Qée'ish, and the church that stands today, built in 1815, is the third on the spot. The mission ran about 26,000 cattle. Pablo Tac, a Luiseño man born at the mission, wrote in Rome around 1835 that a sickness had killed 2,000 of his homeland's 5,000 people, and he worked out a way to write the Luiseño language. When Mexico ended the mission system in 1833, Luiseño families left by the thousands for their home villages. California's first Peruvian pepper tree, planted here in 1830, still grows in the garden. Today six federally recognized Luiseño tribes have reservations in Southern California, and the mission is a parish, museum and retreat center.
places.wiki: Mission San Luis Rey de Francia

places.name: Camp Pendleton
places.text: The open hills along this stretch belong to Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, more than 125,000 acres with 17 miles of coastline, the last major undeveloped stretch of California coast south of Santa Barbara. It was Rancho Santa Margarita y Las Flores until 1942, when the Marines turned it into a training base for World War II.
places.more: In 1841 brothers Pío and Andrés Pico became its first private owners. In the 1860s Pío Pico's brother-in-law, John Forster, paid off Pico's gambling debts in exchange for the deed and turned the rancho into a thriving cattle operation. After droughts, Forster's heirs sold in 1882 to James Flood, whose manager, Richard O'Neill, was rewarded with half the ranch. The rancho's cattle brand still appears in the base logo. The base is named for Major General Joseph Pendleton, who long pushed for a West Coast Marine base. In 1975 it became the first US military base to take in Vietnamese evacuees, more than 50,000 of them. Its wild lands still shelter rare species, among them western snowy plovers and the Pacific pocket mouse.
places.spot: Look for wide open hills with very few buildings.

places.name: Oceanside and its pier
places.text: Oceanside's wooden pier, 1,942 feet long, is the second-longest wooden pier on the West Coast. The first one went up in 1888, the year the city incorporated, and storms have wrecked it again and again. Today's pier, the sixth, opened in 1987. In April 2024 a fire destroyed the old diner at its far end, and rebuilding was expected to begin in 2027.
places.more: The city stands on Payómkawichum land, where the village of Wiyóoya stood at the mouth of the San Luis Rey River. Andrew Jackson Myers settled the original townsite in 1882. When Camp Pendleton opened in World War II, Oceanside jumped from 5,000 people to more than 12,000. On the old Highway 101, Cafe 101 has been a fixture since 1928, and it is often called the oldest cafe on the historic route. Greyhound buses once stopped out front, and it also served as a drive-in and a trailer park. Near the pier stands the house from the movie Top Gun, moved and restored in 2019.

places.name: Santa Margarita River
places.text: The freeway crosses the Santa Margarita River, one of the last free-flowing rivers in Southern California. It runs about 31 miles from near Temecula to the sea, and its lower 10 miles spread into a wide floodplain across Camp Pendleton. The Portolá expedition camped beside it on July 20, 1769, and named it for Saint Margaret of Antioch.
places.more: In 1881 the California Southern Railroad followed the river up Temecula Canyon, crossing it on 241 bridges, and Chinese Americans worked on the line. For decades the Navy and the Fallbrook water district fought over the river's water, and in 2018 the district sold its riverside land, ending a plan more than 60 years old to dam it. In August 2019, Pacific lampreys returned to the river for the first time since 1940, thanks to a rebuilt weir and fishway on the base, the farthest south the species had come back. Endangered least Bell's vireos and southwestern willow flycatchers depend on its streamside habitat to breed.
places.spot: Look for the wide river valley and its trees under the freeway bridge.

places.name: The Surf Line railroad
places.text: The railroad beside the freeway through Camp Pendleton is the Surf Line, named because in places it runs within 100 feet of the Pacific. Finished from Oceanside to Santa Ana in 1888, it became the only line into San Diego from the north after floods wrecked the first route inland. Today it is the second-busiest passenger rail corridor in the United States.
places.more: When the California Southern first built north from San Diego in the early 1880s, its tracks turned inland at Oceanside through Temecula Canyon. In February 1884, more than 40 inches of rain fell in four weeks, washing out two-thirds of the canyon line, and railroad ties were seen floating in the ocean as far as 80 miles away. Today Amtrak's Pacific Surfliner and the Coaster commuter trains share the tracks, and freight trains, often at night, haul loads that include military vehicles for Camp Pendleton. Farther south, at Del Mar, the tracks ride the edge of eroding bluffs 40 feet above the beach, and planners are studying a tunnel that could cost more than $3 billion.
places.spot: Look for a passenger train running alongside the freeway.

places.name: Las Flores and Las Pulgas
places.text: Near the Las Pulgas Road exit stands the Las Flores Adobe, a big U-shaped ranch house built in 1867 and 1868 by Marco Forster and now a National Historic Landmark. It sits where Mission San Luis Rey set up a way station in 1823, halfway to Mission San Juan Capistrano. Las Pulgas means the fleas, after a mission survey party that camped in the canyon and got badly bitten.
places.more: When the Portolá expedition camped in the canyon in 1769, Father Juan Crespí named it for its wild roses, so the fleas came later. Luiseño and Acjachemen people, moved here by the mission, built the station's tile-roofed chapel and hostel around three sides of a square, and sailors used its bell tower to find their way. In April 1838, rival Californio forces fought here over who would govern Alta California. The Pico brothers later ran sheep here until drought ruined the ranch in the 1860s. The Marine Corps and the Camp Pendleton Historical Society began restoring the adobe in 2001, and the society leads occasional tours. Boy Scouts have camped here at Rancho Las Flores since 1974.

places.name: San Clemente Border Patrol checkpoint
places.text: On the lanes toward San Clemente, about seven miles south of that city, stands a permanent Border Patrol checkpoint, one of 33 fixed checkpoints near the Mexican border. Agents may briefly stop and question drivers here without any particular suspicion. The Supreme Court upheld that power in 1976 in United States v. Martinez-Fuerte, a case that began with a stop at this checkpoint.
places.more: The checkpoints stand 25 to 75 miles from the border on major highways, a third layer of enforcement after agents at the line and roving patrols. The 1976 case began when Amado Martinez-Fuerte was stopped here and charged with illegally transporting two passengers who had come in through San Ysidro. The court ruled 7 to 2 that such stops do not violate the Fourth Amendment, even when agents send cars to a second inspection largely on the basis of apparent Mexican ancestry. Critics still argue that the checkpoints are unconstitutional. US citizens need no papers here, but drivers are not allowed to go on until agents are satisfied.

zones.label: Border and South Bay
zones.text: Between the San Ysidro border crossing and Chula Vista, the freeway crosses Kumeyaay land of river valleys, salt ponds and marsh at the south end of San Diego Bay.

zones.label: San Diego Bay and downtown
zones.text: This stretch follows the east side of San Diego Bay through National City, the Navy's piers, Barrio Logan, downtown, the airport and Old Town, where Spanish California began in 1769.

seasons.winter: Most of the year's rain, less than 12 inches on average, falls from December through March.
seasons.summer: Marine layer clouds, most common from May to August, often keep mornings near the coast cool and gray, a pattern locals call May gray and June gloom.

zones.label: Mission Bay to La Jolla
zones.text: Mission Bay's man-made islands, Rose Canyon and its fault, and the slopes of Mount Soledad line this stretch, along with UC San Diego and University City.

zones.label: Torrey Pines to Encinitas
zones.text: A string of coastal lagoons where creeks and rivers meet the sea, Los Peñasquitos, San Dieguito and San Elijo, alternates with the beach towns of Del Mar, Solana Beach and Encinitas.

seasons.summer: Live racing runs at the Del Mar racetrack from July into early September.
seasons.fall: A second Del Mar race meet runs in November.

zones.label: Carlsbad and Oceanside
zones.text: Carlsbad's flower and strawberry fields, three more lagoons, Batiquitos, Agua Hedionda and Buena Vista, and the beach town of Oceanside fill this stretch of Luiseño and Kumeyaay country.

seasons.spring: The Flower Fields bloom from early March into early May, and strawberry picking usually runs from March through July.
seasons.fall: Migrating birds stop at Buena Vista Lagoon, and the strawberry farm's pumpkin season picks up in late September.
seasons.winter: Strawberry plants set out in October give their first berries around the start of the year.

zones.label: Camp Pendleton coast
zones.text: Through Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton the freeway follows the ocean for about 18 miles, past open hills, river valleys and the Surf Line railroad, on land kept for Marine training since 1942.

trivia.q: About how many vehicles enter the United States at the San Ysidro border crossing on a typical day?
trivia.why: About 70,000 vehicles and 20,000 people on foot come north through San Ysidro each day.

trivia.q: In 1915, San Diego offered Charles Hatfield $10,000 to do what?
trivia.why: The self-styled rainmaker was to fill a reservoir, and the 1916 storms that followed broke the Lower Otay Dam.

trivia.q: What did artists paint on the freeway and bridge pillars of Chicano Park?
trivia.why: Chicano Park has the largest collection of outdoor murals in the United States, painted on the concrete pillars.

trivia.q: Which famous airplane was built in San Diego in 1927?
trivia.why: The Spirit of St. Louis was built in San Diego for Charles Lindbergh's 1927 flight across the Atlantic, and the city named its airport Lindbergh Field.

trivia.q: Besides Torrey Pines, the only other wild Torrey pines grow on which island?
trivia.why: A related kind of Torrey pine grows wild in two groves on Santa Rosa Island, off Santa Barbara.

trivia.q: The town of Del Mar was named after what?
trivia.why: Ella Loop named it after Bayard Taylor's poem The Fight of Paso del Mar.

trivia.q: Which famous singer stood at the main gate to greet fans when the Del Mar racetrack opened in 1937?
trivia.why: Bing Crosby helped found the track and welcomed about 15,000 fans on opening day.

trivia.q: What kind of flower blooms across the Carlsbad Flower Fields each spring?
trivia.why: The fields are 55 acres of Giant Tecolote ranunculus, blooming from early March into early May.

trivia.q: In the 1970s, what surprising birds showed up at Buena Vista Lagoon?
trivia.why: Locals thought the flamingos had escaped from the San Diego Zoo, but the zoo said none were missing.

trivia.q: Which TV hero had episodes filmed at Mission San Luis Rey in 1957?
trivia.why: Disney's Zorro series filmed scenes there, with the mission standing in for Mission San Gabriel.

trivia.q: Las Pulgas Road on Camp Pendleton is named after what?
trivia.why: Las pulgas is Spanish for the fleas, which bit a mission survey party that camped in the canyon.

trivia.q: The rare Pacific pocket mouse, which lives on Camp Pendleton, is more closely related to which animal than to mice?
trivia.why: Despite its name, it belongs to the family Heteromyidae, which makes it a closer relative of beavers than of true mice.
